content: I run an online home-goods store with a $72 average order value, a 42% gross margin, and $9 average shipping cost. About 38% of carts are abandoned after shoppers see shipping. I can either offer free shipping above a threshold or run a 15% sitewide discount, but I cannot afford both. Which should I test first, what exact threshold or offer would you use, and how would you measure whether it improved profit rather than just revenue over the next 30 days?

# Test the free-shipping threshold first, at $95

## Why the 15% discount is the weaker bet

At a $72 AOV and 42% gross margin, gross profit is about **$30.24 per order**. (These numbers assume customers currently pay shipping. If you absorb it today, subtract $9 throughout.)

- A 15% discount takes **$10.80 per order** out of margin, leaving about $19.44. That cuts profit per order by roughly **36%**.
- To break even, you'd need **about 56% more orders** ($30.24 ÷ $19.44 = 1.56). That's a very high bar.
- It also discounts every order, including people who would have bought anyway. And it doesn't address your known problem: 38% of carts abandoned at the shipping reveal.

Free shipping above a threshold targets that abandonment point directly. It also pushes cart sizes up instead of shrinking them.

## Why the threshold should be $95

**The break-even math.** Suppose a customer who would have spent $72 adds items to reach the threshold. Each extra dollar earns $0.42 of margin, and you now absorb $9 of shipping. You recover that $9 once the order grows by $9 ÷ 0.42 ≈ **$21.40**. That puts the profit-neutral threshold at about **$93.40**. At $95, every "bumped-up" order is slightly profitable on its own, and every recovered abandoned cart is pure upside.

**Check before you commit.** Pull your order-value distribution for the last 90 days.
- If very few orders fall between $70 and $95, the gap is too large to bridge. Use **$85–$89** instead and rely on conversion lift to cover the difference.
- If more than about 20–25% of orders are **already above $95**, you'll be giving $9 to customers who didn't need the incentive. Factor that subsidy into your expectations. It is the main hidden cost of this test.

**Help customers reach the threshold:**
- Show a progress bar ("You're $18 away from free shipping").
- Add $15–$25 add-on products near cart and checkout. Higher-margin items are best.

## How to measure profit, not just revenue (30 days)

**Setup**
- Run an A/B split by **visitor**, 50/50, using your platform's split-testing tool or an app like Intelligems or Shipscout.
- Control: current shipping.
- Variant: free shipping on orders of $95 or more.
- Don't run other promotions during the test.

**Primary metric: contribution profit per visitor**

> (Revenue − COGS − shipping you absorb − payment fees − discounts − refunds/returns) ÷ unique visitors

Per-visitor numbers capture conversion and AOV together. A variant that raises revenue but loses money will show up as a loss here.

**Secondary metrics**
- Conversion rate
- AOV
- Percentage of orders at or above $95
- Cart abandonment rate at the shipping step
- Shipping cost per order. Bigger orders may cost more than $9 to ship, so use actual label costs.
- Return rate. Watch for people padding carts to qualify and then returning items.

**Decision rule**
- Adopt the threshold if the variant's contribution per visitor beats control with reasonable confidence, roughly 90% or better.
- Keep it only if the return rate is not meaningfully higher.

**Sample size check**
- A 10% lift on a roughly 2–3% conversion rate needs on the order of **15–25k visitors per arm**.
- If 30 days won't get you there, extend the test. Don't call it early.
- Compare full weeks so weekend patterns don't distort the results.

**Follow-up**
- Track repeat purchases from both groups for another 30–60 days.
- Free shipping often improves retention, which would strengthen the case further.
